summary: Patrick Gray, a religious studies professor at Rhodes College, argues in this Martin Center essay that college campuses share features with cults, including intense orientations, bias-reporting systems, emotionally manipulative administrative emails, and odd academic claims. He ultimately concludes that colleges are not cults because cults are fringe phenomena on society's margins, while campus culture is mainstream and influential. He closes by asking whether society will become more like the campus or campus culture will yield to outside forces.
one_line: Patrick Gray compares college orientations, bias-reporting systems, and campus rhetoric to cult tactics, then concludes colleges are not cults but mainstream institutions.
key_facts: Patrick Gray is professor of religious studies at Rhodes College in Memphis, TN.
The essay was published October 27, 2023 by the James G. Martin Center for Academic Renewal.
Over 60 percent of Americans pass through college on their way to adulthood, according to the essay's cited Bureau of Labor Statistics link.
Gray lived in Japan and regularly interacted with recruiters from groups such as Jehovah's Witnesses, Tenchi Seikyo, Mahikari, and Happy Science at train stations.
Gray describes college orientations that begin with a 'love bomb' from aggressively friendly student volunteers and separate students from their families with the phrase 'It's time to say good-bye.'
Gray writes that orientations can last as long as a week and that sleep deprivation is common.
Bias-reporting systems are coordinated by 'Bias Education Response' teams, which Gray says put a pedagogical veneer on a system for monitoring and modifying behavior.
Gray cites Emperor Trajan, who said anonymous tips 'create the worst sort of precedent and are quite out of keeping with the spirit of our age.'
Gray notes that 'cry closets' stocked with stuffed animals and 'puppy rooms' with live animals are offered to stressed students.
Gray cites a Holy Cross professor who identifies Jesus as a masochistic 'drag king' as an example of odd campus ideas.
Gray argues that the key difference between a religion and a cult is that a cult is a fringe phenomenon standing on the margins of mainstream society.
John McWhorter has argued that the preoccupation with social-justice issues among progressives on campus is best understood as a religion.
Gray concludes that 'Sociologically speaking, colleges are not cults.'
Gray closes by noting that in the fourth century a movement emerged from Mediterranean cults to become the official religion of the Roman Empire, and asks whether something similar can happen again.
